Start or STop Anticoagulants Randomised Trial (SoSTART) after spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage CR007-T01v3.0 Version 6.0 23 January 2020 Page 11 of 66 3 SUMMARIES 3.1 PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY Primary research question For adults surviving spontaneous (non-traumatic) symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage with persistent/paroxysmal atrial fibrillation/flutter (AF), does starting full treatment dose oral anticoagulation (OAC) result in a beneficial net reduction of all serious vascular events compared with not starting OAC? Trial design Investigator-led, multicentre, randomised, open, assessor-masked, parallel group, clinical trial of investigational medicinal product (CTIMP) prescribing strategies. We plan for a pilot phase, followed by a safety phase. Objectives Pilot phase: ~30 hospital sites keep screening logs and recruit at least 60 participants >24 hours after spontaneous symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage with AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 to determine the acceptability and feasibility of recruiting the target sample size in a definitive trial in an acceptable timescale. Safety phase: ~60 hospital sites will recruit at least 190 participants to determine whether the risk of recurrent symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage is sufficiently low (non-inferior) to justify a definitive trial. Eligibility criteria Inclusion: Spontaneous symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2. Exclusion: Patient age <18 years. Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within the last 24 hours. Brain imaging that first diagnosed the intracranial haemorrhage is not available. Intracranial haemorrhage is exclusively due to trauma or haemorrhagic transformation of ischaemic stroke. Patient or their doctor is certain about whether to start full dose OAC. Intention to implement the allocated treatment strategy for <1 year. Patient is not registered with a general practitioner. Patient is pregnant, breastfeeding, or of childbearing age and not taking contraception. Lactose intolerance. Patient and carer unable to understand spoken or written English. Previously randomised in SoSTART. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sub-study: MRI must be done after intracranial haemorrhage but before randomisation. Sub-study participants must not have contraindications to MRI. Setting Recruitment in secondary care (inpatient and outpatient services in stroke, general internal medicine, medicine of the elderly, cardiology, neurology and neurosurgery) with follow-up in primary and secondary care. Randomisation Central, web-based randomisation, with 1:1 allocation of intervention: comparator, using a minimisation algorithm.

Start or STop Anticoagulants Randomised Trial (SoSTART) after spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage CR007-T01v3.0 Version 6.0 23 January 2020 Page 12 of 66 Intervention Start long-term (≥1 year) full treatment dose OAC (either a non-vitamin K antagonist direct oral anticoagulant [DOAC] or vitamin K antagonist if a DOAC cannot be used), chosen by the patient’s physician before randomisation. Comparators Do not start OAC (standard clinical practice without OAC may include antiplatelet drug(s) or no antithrombotic drugs). Outcome measures Pilot phase: The proportions of eligible patients who are recruited, unsuitable, or decline to participate; the acceptability of the trial protocol to investigators and patients; and the rate of recruitment per site. Safety phase: Primary outcome: Recurrent, symptomatic, spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage. Exploratory outcomes: All symptomatic serious vascular events (i.e. major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events [MACCE]) including non-fatal stroke and spontaneous subdural haemorrhage, non-fatal myocardial infarction, vascular death, sudden death, or death of unknown cause. Individual symptomatic vascular events. Individual types of fatal events. Dependence according to the modified Rankin Scale. Follow up At least one year after randomisation, using annual questionnaires to participants and their GPs, including review of any medical records and brain imaging relating to outcomes. Sample size We plan to recruit at least 60 participants in a pilot phase and at least 190 participants in a safety phase (12% equivalence margin in the outcome of symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, 1-sided p=0.025 and power 90%).

Start or STop Anticoagulants Randomised Trial (SoSTART) after spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage CR007-T01v3.0 Version 6.0 23 January 2020 Page 13 of 66 3.2 PLAIN ENGLISH SUMMARY† Background to the research • Bleeding within the skull, also known as brain haemorrhage, affects 3 million people in the world each year. • One in five people who survive brain haemorrhage have an irregular heart rhythm called ‘atrial fibrillation’, which puts them at risk of stroke and other blood clots. • Blood-thinning medicines, known as ‘anticoagulant’ drugs, are used in everyday clinical practice to protect people with atrial fibrillation from developing blood clots. However, these drugs also increase the risk of bleeding. • ‘Randomised controlled trials’ showed that anticoagulant drugs benefit people with atrial fibrillation. Randomised controlled trials are the fairest tests of treatments. However, these trials did not include people who had a history of brain haemorrhage. • Recent published studies have observed what happened to people with brain haemorrhage and atrial fibrillation. These studies found that people who started anticoagulant drugs after brain haemorrhage were less likely to die, less likely to suffer blood clots, and were at similar risk of bleeding in comparison to people who did not start these drugs. • However, these studies were not reliable because they were not randomised controlled trials. Aims of the research • We aim to perform a randomised controlled trial involving people with atrial fibrillation who have had a brain haemorrhage. • We want to produce reliable information about whether these people benefit from starting anticoagulant drugs. • These findings would be used to look after people with brain haemorrhage and atrial fibrillation in standard clinical practice in the NHS. Design and methods used • A network of hospital doctors, nurses, and other staff will identify people who survive brain haemorrhage and have atrial fibrillation. • If a patient and their doctor are uncertain about whether to start an anticoagulant drug, they may invite the patient to participate. • Staff will provide the patient, their legal representative, or their nearest relative with information leaflets about this trial. • After consent is given, a patient can undergo an additional detailed magnetic scan of their brain, known as MRI, which would not always happen in standard practice. After the MRI scan, each patient will be allocated at random to either starting or not starting an anticoagulant drug. There is a 1 in 2, or 50%, chance of receiving either strategy. • If the patient is allocated to start anticoagulant drugs, the patient’s doctor will prescribe their choice of anticoagulant drug for the patient. • If the patient is allocated to not start anticoagulant drugs, the patient’s doctor will not prescribe an anticoagulant drug. • We will follow-up all participants for at least one year to determine whether prescribing an anticoagulant drug improves outcome. † INVOLVE. Traumatic intracranial haemorrhage does not provoke the same therapeutic dilemmas as spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage because the risk of recurrence is lower. Extradural haemorrhage occurs after head injury so it is regarded as ‘traumatic’ in origin. 4.1.2 Some people with intracranial haemorrhage have atrial fibrillation, which may cause cerebral or systemic embolism The prevalence of atrial fibrillation (AF) rises with age: in a European population in the early 1990s the overall prevalence of AF was 5.5%, rising from 0.7% at 55–59 years to 17.8% at ≥85 years.9 AF is associated with an increased risk of death of any cause, cardiovascular death, major cardiovascular events, ischaemic stroke, ischaemic heart disease, sudden cardiac death, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and peripheral arterial disease (but not haemorrhagic stroke),10 largely due to embolism of thrombus from the left atrial appendage. Large observational studies have found that the occurrence of intracranial haemorrhage (ICH or subdural haemorrhage) in patients with AF is a risk factor for future cerebral or systemic embolism, independent of CHA2DS2-VASc score.18-21 CHA2DS2-VASc item Score* Congestive heart failure/LV dysfunction 1 Hypertension 1 Age ≥75 years 2 Diabetes mellitus 1 Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism 2 Vascular disease (prior myocardial infarction/peripheral artery disease/aortic plaque) 1 Age 65-74 years 1 Sex category (female) 1 * 1-year risk of cerebral or systemic embolism according to total score: 0 (0.0%), 1 (1.3%), 2 (2.2%), 3 (3.2%), 4 (4.0%), 5 (6.7%), 6 (9.8%), 7 (9.6%), 8 (6.7%), 9 (15.2%) 4.1.3 Primary and secondary prevention of cerebral and systemic embolism in people with AF and no history of intracranial haemorrhage OAC drugs that have been used the longest include the vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), such as warfarin. VKAs reduce the synthesis of functional vitamin K-dependent factors (factor II, FVII, FIX, FX, as well as protein C and protein S) by interfering with the vitamin K redox cycle. Randomised controlled trials involving people with AF without a history of intracranial haemorrhage have shown that full dose VKA OAC drugs (i.e. to achieve target international normalised ratio [INR] 2-3) result in net/overall clinical benefit when used to decrease the risk of cerebral and systemic embolism, despite doubling the risk of intracranial haemorrhage: • A meta-analysis of eight randomised controlled trials found that full dose VKA OAC was superior to antiplatelet drugs for reducing the risk of all stroke and systemic embolism for patients with AF and no history of ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA).22,23 • A meta-analysis of two randomised controlled trials found that VKA OAC was superior to antiplatelet drugs for reducing the risk of all serious vascular events for patients with AF and a history of ischaemic stroke or TIA.23,24 However, VKA OAC is complicated by unpredictable and variable dosage requirements, dietary restrictions, interactions with many other drugs, and the need for close therapeutic drug monitoring to keep the INR in the therapeutic range.

Start or STop Anticoagulants Randomised Trial (SoSTART) after spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage CR007-T01v3.0 Version 6.0 23 January 2020 Page 17 of 66 Newer direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) inhibit an activated clotting factor, either thrombin/FIIa (dabigatran) or FXa (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, and betrixaban), thereby reducing thrombin, fibrin, and clot formation. The pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of DOACs are more predictable than those of the VKAs, so routine monitoring of the anticoagulant effect is not required,25 and they have few drug-drug and drug-food interactions. Randomised controlled trials involving people without a history of intracranial haemorrhage have shown that DOACs are superior to full dose VKA OAC and superior to antiplatelet drugs, when used to prevent cerebral and systemic embolism in patients with AF: • A meta-analysis of four randomised controlled trials of four DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban) found that they were collectively superior to warfarin for reduction of cerebral or systemic embolism (without heterogeneity in sub-groups), all-cause mortality and intracranial haemorrhage, although DOACs did cause more gastrointestinal haemorrhages.26 • A meta-analysis of 10 randomised controlled trials found that factor Xa DOACs were superior to full dose VKA OAC for reducing the risk of strokes and systemic embolic events for patients with AF.27 Factor Xa DOACs also reduce the risk of intracranial haemorrhage,28-30 but dabigatran and rivaroxaban seem to increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding compared to VKAs.31 There are no direct randomised comparisons to indicate whether one factor Xa DOAC is superior to the others27 (although an observational study found apixaban was associated with a lower risk of major haemorrhage requiring hospitalisation than other DOACs and warfarin32). Age does not alter the effect of DOACs compared to warfarin.33,34 • The AVERROES randomised trial found that the DOAC apixaban was superior to aspirin for reducing the risk of stroke or systemic embolism (without increasing the risk of intracranial or extracranial haemorrhage) for patients with AF at increased risk for ischaemic stroke who were not suitable candidates for – or were unwilling to receive – VKA treatment.35 No robust, prospective observational study has shown any benefit from withholding OAC on the basis of a high risk of bleeding36 or a low risk of embolism.37 Other interventions are not superior to full dose OAC. Antiplatelet drugs result in a ~20% relative reduction in the risk of stroke for patients in AF, but full dose OAC is substantially more effective than antiplatelet drugs.23 Left atrial appendage occlusion with the WATCHMAN device (followed by prolonged antiplatelet therapy) is an intervention that was non-inferior38,39 and possibly superior40 to warfarin for the prevention of cerebral and systemic embolism over ~4 years in patients with AF in randomised trials. Guidelines for the management of AF from The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE),41 which concur with other guidelines,42,43 recommend: • Do not offer stroke prevention treatment to people aged <65 years with AF and no risk factors other than their sex (i.e. CHA2DS2-VASc score of 0 for men or 1 for women). • Consider full dose OAC for men with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1, while taking the bleeding risk into account. • Offer full dose OAC to people with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of ≥2, taking bleeding risk into account. • Anticoagulate with a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran etexilate, or rivaroxaban) or a VKA (such as warfarin).

NICE recommends the use of the CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores for risk stratification of patients with AF in general,41 but it is unclear whether full dose OAC should be given to all survivors of intracranial haemorrhage with AF, some survivors according to these risk prediction scores, or none. 4.1.4.1 Full dose oral anticoagulation is associated with better outcome than antiplatelet drugs and no antithrombotic drugs in observational studies In a systematic review of Medline and EMBASE (updated to 31st December 2016),52 we found several observational studies of the outcomes associated with starting vs. not starting OAC after intracranial haemorrhage associated with VKA or DOAC use. Many of these have been small case series (without control groups) involving adults with various indications for full dose OAC, including patients with prosthetic/mechanical heart valve replacements. Given the high risk of thromboembolism with prosthetic heart valves, the dilemma for these patients after intracranial haemorrhage is when – rather than whether – to resume VKA OAC; resumption appears to be associated with overall benefit but the recommended interval has varied from a few days53-56 to at least one month.57 Many of these observational studies have not reported outcomes separately for patients by site of haemorrhage or according to the indication for full dose OAC, which confer different risks of future serious vascular events.47,57-79 Three published studies (and one conference abstract80) have focussed on the outcome for adults with AF and intracranial haemorrhage, stratified by antithrombotic drug use after stroke.21,44,45 The published studies found that starting full dose OAC (almost exclusively with warfarin) was associated with a lower risk of ischaemic stroke and a higher risk of recurrent intracranial haemorrhage (event rates are summarised in the table below). There were associations between starting warfarin and a lower risk of a composite outcome of ischaemic stroke or ICH21 and a composite outcome of any serious vascular event44 (i.e. net clinical benefit). Two of these studies also found that restarting full dose OAC was associated with a reduction in the risk of death of any cause,44,45 and one of them found an association with better functional outcome (probably mediated by reduction in the risk of recurrent stroke).45 One study suggested that a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 6 was a threshold about which there was net benefit and below which there was net harm from OAC.21 One study found that starting warfarin was associated with lower costs due to hospitalisation.81

Randomised trials comparing left atrial appendage occlusion versus antithrombotic treatment for people with AF and a past history of intracranial haemorrhage are ongoing (NCT02426944, NCT02830152). 4.2 RATIONALE FOR THE TRIAL 4.2.1 Guidelines, a systematic review, and expert opinions have confirmed therapeutic uncertainty Recent guidelines and a working party have not found high quality evidence to enable them to make strong recommendations about whether and when to start full dose OAC for people with AF after intracranial haemorrhage.93-95 Our systematic review (updated to 31st December 2016) did not identify any publications of completed randomised controlled trials comparing full dose OAC to other interventions for people with AF after intracranial haemorrhage.52 Several narrative reviews, surveys of experts and debates have been unable to reach agreement on the optimal management of patients in AF with intracranial haemorrhage associated with full dose OAC.96-102 A frequently-cited decision analysis using a Markov model compared full dose OAC with warfarin versus no OAC for a hypothetical patient with AF after ICH.103 This decision analysis was limited by the use of one hospital-based case series for event rates, an absence of data on the effect of full dose OAC on the risk of recurrent ICH, and the assumptions of Markov models, rendering the authors’ conclusions unreliable for use in clinical practice. 4.2.2 Variation in everyday clinical practice Uncertainty about the effects of full dose OAC after intracranial haemorrhage is likely to have contributed to variation in clinical practice around the world. Although 75-96% of patients with intracranial haemorrhage and AF have a CHA2DS2-VASc score of ≥2,18,20,44-47 in the past only 11-33% of these patients have started full dose OAC after intracranial haemorrhage.20,44-46,58 In an observational study of 206 ICH survivors who had taken VKA OAC at ICH presentation in everyday clinical practice in 2004-2013 in six European countries, 29 (14%) restarted full dose OAC, 23 (11%) restarted antiplatelet drugs, and one (0.5%) restarted both; there was evidence of significant variation in the proportion of patients restarting OAC between cohorts104 and this proportion has been lower in Sweden (9-11%),46,105 but higher in Denmark (17%),44 Germany (24%),45 the USA (48%),78 and Japan (91%).106 A survey of neurosurgeons found that the majority relied on intuition or past experience, rather than the available evidence, when making these decisions.107 4.2.3 Recent evidence that full dose oral anticoagulation appears to be a promising intervention for people with AF after intracranial haemorrhage Associations observed in recently-published non-randomised studies suggest that starting full dose OAC may be superior to not starting OAC in patients with intracranial haemorrhage (especially ICH) and indications (especially AF) for full dose OAC (see 4.1.4.1 above on page 18). ICH.111 Use of VKA OAC, but perhaps not DOAC, seems to be associated with an increase in the number of brain microbleeds on repeat MRI after one year.112,113 Brain microbleeds are risk factors for
